Instructor and TA material. Not rendered into the student site.

## Setup

- **15 envelopes**, each with a printed image of its 6 cards on the outside, and
  inside: the 6 physical cards, the fact slip, and a reference card.
- Groups of 6 (TAs fill gaps). ~72 enrolled, so expect 12 full groups.
- **Roles come from the card each player draws** --- there is no separate role
  deal. Black = Sage (truth), Red = Trickster (lies).
- Because the card image on the envelope is public, **the number of Tricksters is
  public too**: count the red cards. Students need that number, or the puzzle has
  no unique answer (all-Sage and all-Trickster produce identical answers).

## The four rules

1. Sages answer truthfully. Tricksters must invert every answer.
2. **Two questions total**, agreed by the group. Every player answers both.
3. **Each question must be true of at least one of the six visible cards.*
   Without this, "is your card an ace?" in a packet with no ace makes every
   "yes" a proven lie and the game ends in one question. With it, no packet is
   solvable in one question and every packet is solvable in two.
4. **During the debate round nobody may state their own card or role.** Reason
   only from the answers already given. Tricksters are constrained, not
   adversarial --- they want the group to succeed. Say this out loud; students
   arriving from Werewolf will assume the opposite, and in Packet 12 the
   Tricksters are 5 of 6 and could simply outvote the good questions.

## What makes a question work

Each player answers about their own card, so for a property $P$:

$$\text{says yes} \iff P(\text{card}) \ne \text{red}(\text{card})$$

That predicts the dead questions:

| Question | Result | Why |
|---|---|---|
| "Is your card red?" | everyone says no | black isn't red and says so; red is red and denies it |
| "Is your card black?" | everyone says yes | same collapse, inverted |
| "Are you a Trickster?" | everyone says no | same question as "is your card red?" |

The move that works: **two properties that cannot both be true of one card.** A
black card is a spade or a club, never both, so a Sage says yes to at most one.
A Trickster's truth is no to both, and they invert both --- so they say yes
twice.

> **Yes to both $\Rightarrow$ Trickster. Yes to at most one $\Rightarrow$ Sage.**

**Keep this off the reference card.** It is the discovery. The card tells them
only to ask about the card rather than its colour --- necessary, since with two
questions a wasted round is fatal. **Hint to deploy if a group stalls:** *"try
two properties that cannot both be true of the same card."* That is enough to
unlock every packet without handing over the conclusion.

Rank questions work too, but they are weaker alone: suit determines colour,
rank does not, so a "yes" to a rank question could be a truthful black card
with the property or a lying red card without it. 14 of the 15 packets have a
working rank-based pair; Packet 14 is the exception and needs suits.

Trickster count = number of red cards. Every pair below was checked by

consistent answer.

|--:|---|---|--:|---|---|

| 2 | 8S 5H KS 4H 9D 5H | Exactly two players have spades. | 4 | "a heart" + "a diamond" | "a diamond" + "5 or lower" |

| 6 | AS 6S 10H JC 6D 5C | Exactly two cards are sixes. | 2 | "a spade" + "a club" | "a spade" + "a face card" |
| 7 | 9H 5D JC JH KS 2D | Exactly two cards are jacks. | 4 | "a spade" + "a club" | "a heart" + "9 or higher" |
| 8 | 6D 8S 3H 10D 5S KC | Spades equals diamonds. | 3 | "a spade" + "a club" | "a spade" + "a face card" |
| 9 | AD QD 9S 9D 2C 7S | Exactly three players have diamonds. | 3 | "a spade" + "a club" | "a spade" + "an even number" |
| 10 | 2H 7D 5D JS 10C 6C | All clubs are even-numbered. | 3 | "a spade" + "a club" | "a club" + "a face card" |
| 11 | 10S 4S 10S AC KD QC | Exactly two copies of 10S in play. | **1** | "a spade" + "a club" | "a spade" + "an ace" |
| 12 | KH QH 3D KD QS 8D | Kings equals queens. | **5** | "a heart" + "a diamond" | "a heart" + "a face card" |
| 13 | QS 10H 8C 9S 3C 6H | No player has a diamond. | 2 | "a spade" + "a club" | "a spade" + "5 or lower" |
| 14 | 3S 2C 7D 6S 3S 5S | Exactly four players have spades. | **1** | "a spade" + "a club" | *none --- must use suits* |
| 15 | 8D 9H 2S AS 4D 4C | Exactly two cards are fours. | 3 | "a spade" + "a club" | "a club" + "an ace" |

### Notes on individual packets

- **Packet 12** --- the to-do list offered a second fact, *"all spade cards are
  even."* It is **ill-defined**: the only spade is Q♠, and a Queen is neither
  even nor odd. Check the slip in that envelope; if it carries this fact,
  replace it with the kings/queens one.
- **Packets 11 and 14** have a single Trickster and **12 has five**. All three
  still have exactly one solution, so they work as-is --- they are just faster
  or stranger. Packet 12 is worth calling on in the debrief: with 5 liars,
  majority vote gives that group confidently the wrong answer.
- To even the splits later, two card swaps fix each: 11 → `AC`, `QC` become
  `AH`, `QD` (3/3); 12 → `KH`, `QH` become `KS`, `QC` (3/3); 14 → `2C` becomes
  `2H` (2/4, the best possible while keeping four spades). All facts stay true.

## Debrief

Ask a group that used a colour question what happened, then a group that used
mutually exclusive questions. The contrast is the point: one question carried
no information at all, the other settled six roles.

Then the bridge to the rest of the hour. Two claims about the room:

- *"Priya is a Trickster"* --- settled by finding a contradiction. Certain.
- *"Most questions were about the same card"* --- settled by counting. Supported.

Both are arguments. This course is the first kind. Do not oversell the
connection; it gets earned in lecture 3, when a boolean mask turns out to be a
predicate evaluated over rows.

## Reference card

Print one per group, half-page.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Sages & Tricksters

**Goal.** Together, work out who is a Sage and who is a Trickster.

**Setup.** You each draw one card and keep it hidden. **Black = Sage**, you
always tell the truth. **Red = Trickster**, you always lie. The six cards are
printed on the envelope, so everyone can see how many Tricksters there are ---
count the red ones. The fact on the slip is true.

**Round 1 --- Questions.** As a group, agree on **two** yes/no questions. Every
player answers both. Each question must be true of **at least one** of the six
cards you can see.

**Round 2 --- Debate.** Compare the answers and look for contradictions. You may
**not** say what card you hold or which role you are. Reason only from the
answers.

**Round 3 --- Conclusion.** Agree on who is which, then reveal.

**Asking well.** You get two questions. Spend them carefully.

1. Ask about your **card** --- its suit, or its rank.
2. Do **not** ask about its colour. Try it and see what happens.
